newsitem.title: USA: Pilot's trial set to begin despite discharge bid.
newsitem.headline: Pilot's trial set to begin despite discharge bid.

text.p: The court-martial of the U.S. Air Force's first woman B-52 pilot on a criminal charge of adultery is set to begin on Tuesday despite her bid for a discharge, sources close to the case said on Sunday.

Attorneys for Lt. Kelly Flinn will ask the Air Force on Monday to honourably discharge the 26-year-old lieutenant, but it is not certain that the request will be granted or even how quickly the service might act on it.

Flinn, who is single, is scheduled to be court-martialed at Minot Air Force Base, North Dakota, on charges of adultery and fraternisation. She has acknowledged an affair with a married civilian and is also accused of having sex with a lower-ranking enlisted man.

Under Air Force procedures, Flinn's request must pass through several chains of command before Air Force Secretary Sheila Widnall can decide on whether to grant it. The request may be turned down at any of those various levels of command.
In the meantime it was unclear whether the judge in the case, Col. Dennis Kansala, will halt the court-martial while the Air Force mulls Flinn's bid.
"There could be some type of a hold, but again, the judge in the case will have to look at the relative merits in the case," an Air Force spokesman told Reuters.
The spokesman would not comment on the likelihood of the Air Force granting Flinn's request for an honourable discharge.

Flinn's lawyers have already tried twice over the past three days to delay the court-martial, but Kansala has rejected those attempts. A spokeswoman for Flinn's lawyers would not comment on whether they would again try to delay the court martial.
"The trial is still scheduled to begin on Tuesday," the spokeswoman said in a telephone interview from Minot.
In a statement released on Saturday, Flinn said an honourable discharge would spare both her and the Air Force any further embarrassment over the issue.
Conviction of adultery in a military trial is punishable by penalties ranging up to dishonourable discharge and possible fines and imprisonment.
Defence Secretary William Cohen declined comment on Sunday on Flinn's bid to avoid court-martial this week because the case could eventually come before him.

But Cohen, interviewed on the CBS programme "Face the Nation," said it would be appropriate for the U.S. armed services to review their policies against fraternisation to ensure no sexual bias exists.
Critics have argued that Flinn's case highlights a double standard in the way the U.S. Armed Forces treats the issue of adultery among its male and female staff.
